# Question 1

The trend I chose to look into that affected the 2026 Midterm election was the mid-decade redistricting. By May 2026, nine states (Alabama, California, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Texas, and Utah) had redrawn their congressional maps (NCSL). While each of the states had different reasons for the mid-decade change (legislature, voters, court order/rulings, or constitutional schedule) these maps would be enacted in the 2026 midterms, thus setting up a change in constitutes and demographics for the districts in these states.

I found it interesting that a number of house races were running on lines that did not exist in 2024. The trend also answers a question that I and many others had going into November, would the new lines deliver the seats their drafters projected? In June 2026, the National Conference of State Legislatures estimated that Republicans could gain up to 17 seats and Democrats up to six, under the new maps. This data analysis showcases the results of the 2026 Midterms and highlights the redrawn districts.

Below is the beginning of my analysis on these districts, outlined with starter maps that show the change in districts and party. I used the Census Bureau’s congressional district files for the 119th congress for the 2024 lines. For 2026, I used each state’s enacted plan from the state website. I used Congress.gov to confirm representative parties from 2024 and the Associated Press for 2026 (in districts that were still too close to call, I used predictions or the current majority of votes). Working in R with libraries like sf, dplyr, mapview, ggplot, and leaflet I mapped all of the states that redrew for the 2026 midterms adding a slider for a visual of the change from 2024 to 2026.

As this is only a start of a wider project I would like to examine, I would add demographic data to look into demographic shifts in the redrawn districts using by overlaying census tracts within the districts and pulling the most recent American Community Survey data. To further this idea, I would use Python and a random forest regression to predict trends ahead of the 2028 elections.

```{r}
library(sf)
library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(mapview)
library(leaflet)
```

# CALIFORNIA

```{r}
CA2024 = st_read("/cktportfolio/electiondatagit/electiondata/Congressional_Districts.shp")


CA2026shp = st_read("/cktportfolio/electiondatagit/AB604/AB604.shp")

CAresults26 = read_excel("/cktportfolio/electiondatagit/electiondata/CA2026.xlsx")
CAresults26$DISTRICT = sprintf("%02d", as.integer(CAresults26$DISTRICT))

CA2026 = left_join(CA2026shp,CAresults26, by = "DISTRICT" )
```

```{r}
ggplot(data = CA2024) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = PARTY), color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("D" = "blue3", "R" = "red3"),
    name = "California 2024 Districts",
    na.value = "grey80"  # Colors any missing/other values grey
  ) +
  theme_void()


ggplot(data = CA2026) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = PARTY), color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("D" = "blue3", "R" = "red3"),
    name = "California 2026 Districts",
    na.value = "grey80"  
  ) +
  theme_void()

CAmap2024 <- mapview(
  CA2024,
  zcol = "PARTY",
  col.regions = c("blue3", "red3"),
  na.color = "grey80",
  color = "white", lwd = 0.2,
  layer.name = "California 2024 Districts",
  map.types = "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas",
  popup = FALSE
)

CAmap2026 <- mapview(
  CA2026,
  zcol = "PARTY",
  col.regions = c("blue3", "red3"),
  na.color = "grey80",
  color = "white", lwd = 0.2,
  layer.name = "California 2026 Districts",
  map.types = "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas",
  popup = FALSE
)

swipe <- CAmap2026 | CAmap2024
if (inherits(swipe, "mapview")) swipe <- swipe@map   

swipe |>
  addControl(html = "<b>California 2026 Districts</b>", position = "topright") |>
  addControl(html = "<b>California 2024 Districts</b>", position = "topleft")


```

```{r}

selected <- c("01", "02", "03", "06", "22", "41", "48")

CA2026$highlight <- ifelse(CA2026$DISTRICT %in% selected,
                           CA2026$PARTY,
                           "Not Redrawn for 2026")

ggplot(data = CA2026) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = highlight), color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("D" = "blue3", "R" = "red3", "Not Redrawn for 2026" = "grey85"),
    labels = c("Redrawn, won by Democrat", "Not Redrawn for 2026"),
    name = "CA Redrawn Districts",
    na.value = "grey80"
  ) +
  theme_void()
```

# UTAH

```{r}
UT2024shp = st_read("/cktportfolio/electiondatagit/electiondata/tl_2024_49_cd119/tl_2024_49_cd119.shp")

UTresults26 = read_excel("/cktportfolio/electiondatagit/electiondata/UT2026results.xlsx")



UT2026  = left_join(UTAH2026shp, UTresults26, by = "DISTRICT")

```

```{r}
ggplot(data = UTAH2024) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = PARTY), color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("D" = "blue3", "R" = "red3"),
    name = "UT 2024 Districts",
    na.value = "grey80"  # Colors any missing/other values grey
  ) +
  theme_void()


ggplot(data = UT2026) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = PARTY), color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("D" = "blue3", "R" = "red3"),
    name = "UT 2026 Districts",
    na.value = "grey80"  # Colors any missing/other values grey
  ) +
  theme_void()

UTmap2024 <- mapview(
  UTAH2024,
  zcol = "PARTY",
  col.regions = c( "red3"),
  na.color = "grey80",
  color = "white", lwd = 0.2,
  layer.name = "Utah 2024 Districts",
  map.types = "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas",
  popup = FALSE
)

UTmap2026 <- mapview(
  UT2026,
  zcol = "PARTY",
  col.regions = c("blue3"),
  na.color = "grey80",
  color = "white", lwd = 0.2,
  layer.name = "Utah 2026 Districts",
  map.types = "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas",
  popup = FALSE
)


swipe <- UTmap2026 | UTmap2024
if (inherits(swipe, "mapview")) swipe <- swipe@map   

swipe |>
  addControl(html = "<b>Utah 2026 Districts</b>", position = "topright") |>
  addControl(html = "<b>Utah 2046 Districts</b>", position = "topleft")


```

```{r}
  map.types = "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas",
  popup = FALSE
)

NCmap2026 <- mapview(
  NC2026,
  zcol = "PARTY",
  col.regions = c("blue3", "red3"),
  na.color = "grey80",
  color = "white", lwd = 0.2,
  layer.name = "North Carolina 2026 Districts",
  map.types = "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas",
  popup = FALSE
)

NCswipe <- NCmap2026 | NCmap2024
if (inherits(NCswipe, "mapview")) NCswipe <- NCswipe@map

NCswipe |>
  addControl(html = "<b>North Carolina 2024 Districts</b>", position = "topleft") |>
  addControl(html = "<b>North Carolina 2026 Districts</b>", position = "topright")
```

```{r}
selected = c(1, 3)

NC2026$highlight <- ifelse(as.integer(NC2026$DISTRICT) %in% selected, NC2026$PARTY, "Other")

ggplot(data = NC2026) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = highlight), color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("D" = "blue3", "R" = "red3", "Not Redrawn for 2026" = "grey85"),
    labels = c("Redrawn, won by Democrat", "Redrawn, won by Republican"),
    name = "North Carolina Redrawn Districts",
    na.value = "grey80"
  ) +
  theme_void()
```

# Question 2

As a person who thrives in the numbers, the visuals, and the tools to make data understandable for the public, working for a nonpartisan organization touches on a core value, that the data and an unbiased presentation of the data comes first. In my undergraduate degree, I concentrated in Conflict Resolution. This led me to study divisive international disputes when I lived in Belfast, Northern Ireland. In Belfast, I examined data related the the Troubles and discovered that while there are many ways maps can divide people, they can also contribute to sourcing unity.

Both sides of the conflict, Protestants and Catholics, experienced levels of violence, however, the number of deaths increased significantly when looking at lower income neighborhoods. My report discovered that the two highest death rates were in Whiterock (a predominantly Catholic neighborhood) at 73.53 and Crumlin (a predominately Protestant neighborhood) at 72.7, both of which had the highest social deprivation scores at 74.9 and 78.07 respectively (Faye et al, 1998 and Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency, 2001). All this to say, in this tense political climate, our discipline matters more than ever. I believe that the work being done at the Cook Political Report is vital to informing the public, no matter their political party, about the state of our country.

Within the Washington D.C. ecosystem, I believe the Cook Political Report aids in informing campaigns, members of congress, lobbyists, reporters, all important players in the ecosystem who start from the same point, our data. I would view working at the Cook Political report as upholding the promise made in its founding in 1984 to showcase that the facts will look the same from either side of the aisle.
